System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) with 50 different elements. Findings: XGBoost and Random Forest models achieved 97% accuracy in predicting solid solution phases; XGBoost model achieved 86% accuracy in predicting all 11 phase categories; The inclusion of IM phases had a more pronounced impact on accuracy compared to the inclusion of AM phases; Mixing enthalpy and VEC are important features for predicting phase stability in HEAs; Atomic radius is a effective descriptor for distinguishing between BCC and AM phases. Mechanism: The authors propose that the machine learning models can learn the complex relationships between the features and the phases of HEAs, allowing for accurate predictions. Limitations: The dataset is imbalanced, with some phase categories having more records than others. Future work: The authors suggest that future work should focus on exploring the use of other machine learning models and features to improve the accuracy of phase predictions. Paper card. Question: Can a phase prediction method for high-entropy alloys (HEAs) be developed by integrating a criterion and machine learning recommendation method?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs). Findings: The proposed phase prediction of HEAs (PPH) achieves an average prediction accuracy of 91.6% in all HEAs.; The PPH achieves an average prediction accuracy of 94.3% in quinary HEAs.; The PPH achieves an average prediction accuracy of 93.1% in senary HEAs.; The PPH achieves an average prediction accuracy of 95.8% in septenary HEAs.. Mechanism: The PPH combines the advantages of the criterion of SS and MLRM, where the criterion of SS has strong interpretability and generalization and requires only a small amount of training samples.. Limitations: The performance of the meta-learner in traditional meta-learning is not ideal, and the KNN does not fully consider the information of the left and right nearest neighbors of every sample.. Future work: The PPH can also provide a research foundation in other material fields.. Quote: "The comprehensive properties of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are highly-dependent on their phases."
